methodology.weight: Whole-fruit examples in grams, including natural peel, shell and seeds unless noted. A source may report a range, cultivar or sample mean. Chosen examples are not species averages or record comparisons. Undocumented weights are null and excluded from arithmetic.
methodology.flavorRatings: Burrow editorial ratings from 1 to 10, interpreting descriptions of ripe fruit: 1 barely sweet/tart, 5 moderate, 10 very sweet/tart. Not Brix, sugar grams, laboratory acidity, health scores or tastiness judgments. Breadfruit is rated at the mature cooking stage, plantain ripe and cooked, and olive after curing; weights remain whole fruits before cooking or curing. Cultivar, ripeness and personal perception change flavor.
methodology.availability: Burrow editorial findability bands, 1 to 5, for fresh fruit beyond its home region: 1 local harvest/specialist growers; 2 mostly regional/seasonal; 3 specialty markets; 4 regional staple traded abroad; 5 widely traded. Not a country count, current store inventory, conservation status or price. Based on described cultivation and trade, with no implied worldwide census.
methodology.geography: Origin or cultural/cultivation association, not an exhaustive distribution. Map pins mark representative places within the stated region, not a precisely known birthplace. Ancient origins and some species boundaries remain debated.
methodology.images: Individually credited Commons photos. Stored as resized JPEGs for offline play; no botanical drawings or generated substitutes.
methodology.catalog: Fruit cards include distinct species and familiar market types or cultivar groups, such as nectarines, satsumas and golden kiwifruit; the card count is not a count of unique species.
methodology.size: Approximate longest dimension of one whole fruit body in centimetres: length for elongated fruit, diameter for round or flattened fruit. Excludes stems, leaves, crowns and projecting hairs or spines. Coconut includes its outer husk; cape gooseberry excludes its papery husk; cashew apple excludes the attached nut. Rounded examples are editorial selections within documented dimensions or named cultivar measurements, not species averages, maximum-size rankings or measurements of the pictured specimens. Source ranges and cultivar scope remain in each profile. Size and weight examples may come from different specimens. Collection order uses size, with alphabetical ties; weight-based games continue to use documented weights.

cards.name: Jamun
cards.fact: Jamun can stain your tongue purple with juice from its dark skin and flesh.

size.note: The published 0.5–2 inch length is converted to centimetres; the page's 'm' in the metric parenthesis is a unit typo.

cards.name: Rose Apple
cards.flavor: Mild sweetness with a rose-like scent
cards.fact: A ripe rose apple smells floral, and its loose seeds may rattle inside when it is shaken.

size.note: Body length, excluding the leafy calyx.

cards.name: Wax Apple
cards.fact: Wax apples look like shiny little bells and are not members of the apple family.
cards.imageAlt: Pink wax apples and a cut half showing pale flesh

size.note: The source gives width 4.5–5.4 cm and length 3.4–5 cm; the widest axis is used.

cards.name: Ambarella
cards.texture: Crisp to soft around a fibrous stone
cards.fact: An ambarella's central stone is covered with tough fibers that reach into the flesh.

weight.note: A large-fruit example of about 500 g; Morton reports some Pacific island fruit exceeding this size.

cards.imageAlt: Whole and cut ambarella fruits showing green skin and fibrous seeds

size.note: Fruit-body length, excluding the stalk.

cards.name: Jocote
cards.texture: Juicy flesh around a large stone
cards.fact: Jocotes can be red, yellow or purple when ripe and grow on thick, knobbly branches.

size.note: Length of a whole purple-mombin fruit.

cards.name: Tamarind
cards.texture: Sticky pulp inside a brittle pod
cards.fact: Tamarind is a fruit in a pod, making it a relative of peas and beans.

size.note: One complete pod; the published 2–7 inch range is converted using 2.54 cm per inch.

cards.name: Cashew Apple
cards.fact: The cashew nut grows below the swollen stalk called the cashew apple.

size.note: The fleshy cashew apple only, excluding the attached nut and its shell.

cards.name: Surinam Cherry
cards.fact: Surinam cherries have deep ribs that make them look like tiny pumpkins.

size.note: Across one flattened, ribbed fruit.

cards.name: Grumichama
cards.fact: Grumichama has dark purple skin and pale flesh, even though it is often called Brazil cherry.
cards.imageCreator: No machine-readable author provided. B.navez assumed (based on copyright claims).

size.note: Across the flattened fruit body; the stalk and sepals are excluded.

cards.name: Acerola
cards.fact: Acerola resembles a small cherry but belongs to a different plant family.
cards.imageAlt: Two bright red acerola fruits growing among green leaves

size.note: Across one whole lobed fruit, excluding the stalk.

cards.name: Miracle Fruit
cards.texture: Thin pulp around a large seed
cards.fact: Miracle fruit contains a protein that can temporarily make sour foods taste sweet.

size.note: The reference describes red fruits 2 cm long.

cards.name: Prickly Pear
cards.fact: Prickly pears grow on flat cactus pads and can carry tiny prickles even when the larger spines are absent.
cards.imageCreator: No machine-readable author provided. Hippocampus~commonswiki assumed (based on copyright claims).

size.note: Kew's description gives length 5–9 cm and diameter 3–6 cm; projecting spines are excluded.

cards.name: Pepino
cards.fact: Pepino tastes a little like melon, but it belongs to the tomato and potato family.
cards.imageAlt: Whole pale pepino with purple stripes

size.note: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria describes fruit reaching 10 cm long; 8 cm is an illustrative body-length example.

cards.name: Breadfruit
cards.origin: New Guinea and the Pacific; shaped by cultivation

location.label: New Guinea and the Pacific; shaped by cultivation

cards.flavor: Starchy and potato-like when cooked mature
cards.texture: Firm and starchy before full ripeness
cards.fact: Breadfruit gets its name from the bread-like texture of its cooked flesh.

weight.note: A 1,500 g whole-fruit example within the reported 250–6,000 g range. Firm mature breadfruit is commonly cooked before eating.

cards.imageAlt: Large green breadfruit showing its patterned skin on the tree

size.note: The reference covers many shapes and cultivars; this is a 20 cm example, not an average.

cards.name: Grapefruit
cards.fact: Grapefruit began as a cross between a pomelo and a sweet orange.

weight.note: The Marsh grapefruit cultivar averaged 450 g at Lindcove in 1975–1983 in a UCANR comparison. A site and cultivar example, not a species average.

size.note: Diameter of a whole rounded grapefruit with its rind.

cards.name: Pomelo
cards.flavor: Gentle citrus sweetness with a tang
cards.texture: Large juice sacs beneath thick pith
cards.fact: A pomelo has a thick, spongy layer of white pith under its skin.

weight.note: A 1,000 g whole-fruit example within the reported 260–1,950 g cultivar range. Cultivars and growing conditions change size.

size.note: A rounded pomelo example, including the thick rind.

cards.name: Mandarin
cards.texture: Tender segments with a loose peel
cards.fact: Mandarins are ancestors of many other citrus fruits, including sweet oranges.

weight.note: Rounded from 108.3 g for the US Furr mandarin cultivar sampled at Exeter on 17 October 2010. A cultivar sample, not an average for all mandarins.

size.note: Morton's Willow-leaf mandarin is 5–6.25 cm wide and 4.5–5.7 cm tall; the wider axis is used.

cards.name: Clementine
cards.origin: Algerian cultivation heritage; mandarin and sweet-orange ancestry

location.label: Algerian cultivation heritage; mandarin and sweet-orange ancestry

cards.flavor: Sweet citrus with a mild tang
cards.fact: A clementine combines mandarin and sweet-orange ancestry. It is one of several kinds of easy-peeling citrus.

weight.note: Rounded from 77.9 g, the whole-fruit mean for sample 47.3 (loose clementines) in the UK 2013 sampling report. Includes peel and seeds; one retail sample.

cards.sourceFile: Clementines whole, peeled, half and sectioned.jpg

size.note: Morton's Clementine cultivar description gives height 5–7 cm and width 5–6.1 cm; the longer axis is used.

cards.name: Tangerine
cards.origin: Asian mandarin ancestry; name linked to Tangier trade

location.label: Asian mandarin ancestry; name linked to Tangier trade

cards.texture: Juicy segments under a loose rind
cards.fact: The name tangerine is linked to Tangier in Morocco, once an important port for shipping these fruits.

weight.note: Rounded from 151.1 g, the whole-fruit mean for sample 47.1 (Jaffa juicy tangerines) in the UK 2013 sampling report. Includes peel and seeds; one retail sample.

cards.imageAlt: Peeled tangerine halves showing their orange segments

size.note: Morton's Dancy tangerine example has width 5.7–7.5 cm and height 4–5.4 cm; the wider dimension is used.

cards.name: Satsuma
cards.origin: Japanese cultivation heritage; Asian citrus ancestry

location.label: Japanese cultivation heritage; Asian citrus ancestry

cards.fact: Satsumas are a type of mandarin, known for a very loose peel and fruit that is often seedless.

weight.note: Rounded from 94.3 g, the whole-fruit mean for sample 47.7 (loose satsumas) in the UK 2013 sampling report. Includes peel; one retail sample.

cards.sourceFile: Satsuma mandarins - San Francisco, CA - DSC02398.jpg

size.note: Morton's Owari satsuma is 1.5–2.75 inches wide and 1.5–2.5 inches tall. The wider axis is used; the inconsistent metric width conversion is replaced using 2.54 cm per inch.

cards.name: Blood Orange
cards.fact: Blood oranges are sweet-orange varieties whose red flesh gets its color from anthocyanin pigments.

weight.note: A reported 196 g mean for the Moro blood-orange cultivar in a comparative study published in 2022. Other cultivars and harvests differ.

size.note: Uses the sweet-orange species diameter range; this is an illustrative blood-orange example, not a blood-cultivar measurement.

cards.name: Kumquat
cards.flavor: Sweet peel around a sour center
cards.texture: Thin edible peel and juicy pulp
cards.fact: A kumquat reverses the usual citrus surprise: its peel is sweet while the inside is much more tart.

weight.note: A rounded 16 g example within the reported 11–20 g range for the Puchimaru kumquat cultivar. This is a cultivar example, not a fixed size for every kumquat.

size.note: Morton's rounded Meiwa example is about 4 cm across; other kumquat types can be more elongated.

cards.name: Nectarine
cards.flavor: Sweet and tangy, like a peach
cards.fact: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach, not a cross between a peach and a plum.

weight.note: A reported 170 g mean for the Nectaross nectarine cultivar in a 2021 fruit study. A cultivar sample, not an average for all nectarines.

size.note: Uses the peach species' usual cultivated diameter range; nectarines are smooth-skinned peach varieties, not a separate size class.

cards.name: Cantaloupe
cards.scientificName: Cucumis melo, Cantalupensis and Reticulatus Groups
cards.origin: Long cultivation in West Asia; deeper melon origins debated

location.label: Long cultivation in West Asia; deeper melon origins debated

cards.texture: Soft, juicy flesh inside a firm rind
cards.fact: The netted melon often called cantaloupe in North America is a muskmelon; European cantaloupes can have a different rind.

weight.note: A 1,500 g whole-fruit example within the reported 500–5,000 g cantaloupe range. Includes rind and seeds; varieties vary greatly.

cards.sourceFile: Cucumis melo var. reticulatus (photo by Scott Bauer).jpg
cards.imageCreator: USDA photo by Scott Bauer. Image Number K7355-11.

size.note: Iowa State's harvest guide lists muskmelon/cantaloupe at 5–10 inches diameter; converted to centimetres for a rounded example.

cards.name: Honeydew Melon
cards.origin: West Asian and Mediterranean cultivation heritage

location.label: West Asian and Mediterranean cultivation heritage

cards.texture: Smooth rind around juicy, usually pale-green flesh
cards.fact: Honeydew and cantaloupe are different groups of the same melon species.

weight.note: A 2,700 g whole-fruit example within the reported 1,800–3,600 g honeydew range. Includes rind and seeds, not just edible flesh.

size.note: The longest body dimension of a round to slightly oval honeydew.

cards.name: Date
cards.origin: Middle East; ancient cultivation around the Persian Gulf

location.label: Middle East; ancient cultivation around the Persian Gulf

cards.availabilityBand: Fresh ripe: regional staple traded abroad; dried dates are more widespread
cards.flavor: Deep, caramel-like sweetness when fully ripe
cards.texture: Soft or chewy flesh around a hard seed
cards.fact: Dates grow in large hanging clusters on palms; each fruit has one long, hard seed.

weight.note: Rounded from a reported 15.97 g whole-fruit mean for Medjool dates, including the seed, in an Egyptian horticultural study. Cultivar and ripening stage affect weight.

cards.sourceFile: Mazafati dates - whole, halved and seed.jpg

size.note: One date fruit with its skin and stone, excluding the stalk.

cards.name: Cranberry
cards.texture: Firm skin and crisp, juicy flesh
cards.fact: American cranberries grow on low, trailing vines, rather than on trees.

weight.note: Rutgers describes the Welker American cranberry cultivar as averaging 2 g per berry. A cultivar example; other cranberries differ.

size.note: NC State describes a half-inch round fruit; 1.27 cm is rounded to 1.3 cm. This is one berry, not a cluster.

cards.name: Gooseberry
cards.texture: Thin skin and juicy flesh with small seeds
cards.fact: Despite their names, the gooseberry and Cape gooseberry belong to different plant families.

weight.note: Rounded from a 3.2 g mean for the Konsul gooseberry cultivar in a South Urals study published in 2019. A studied cultivar, not a species average.

size.note: The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network describes berries reaching about 25 mm across; this is an illustrative 2 cm example.

cards.name: Blackcurrant
cards.texture: Small, dark berries with juicy pulp
cards.fact: Blackcurrants are often turned into juice and jam, where their strong flavor stands out.

weight.note: The Titania blackcurrant cultivar averaged 1.0 g per berry in the 2017 Montana WARC trial. A harvest and cultivar example.

cards.imageAlt: Close-up of glossy blackcurrants in a cluster

size.note: Flora of China gives 0.8–1 cm, occasionally 1.4 cm, for the rounded fruit; one berry is compared.

cards.name: Redcurrant
cards.fact: Redcurrants hang in strings of translucent berries that can look like tiny red beads.

weight.note: Rounded to a whole gram from the Rovada redcurrant mean of 0.8 g in the 2017 Montana WARC trial. Coarse whole-gram rounding for a very small berry.

size.note: One berry, using the published 8–12 mm range; not an entire strig.

cards.name: Mulberry
cards.flavor: Rich berry sweetness with a tang
cards.texture: Tender clustered fruit that stains easily
cards.fact: Mulberries grow on trees, while similar-looking blackberries grow on canes.

weight.note: Rounded from 3.85 g, the average fruit weight across studied black-mulberry genotypes in a 2018 paper; individual genotype means ranged from 1.79 to 5.69 g.

size.note: The black-mulberry reference describes compound fruits about 2.5 cm across; other mulberry species differ.

cards.name: Avocado
cards.texture: Creamy flesh around one large seed
cards.fact: An avocado is botanically a berry with one large seed, even though it is usually eaten in savory dishes.

weight.note: A 250 g whole-fruit example within the reported 100–1,000 g range. Includes skin and seed; cultivar sizes differ widely.

cards.imageAlt: Whole and halved avocado showing green flesh and a large brown seed
cards.sourceFile: Branch and fruit of the Maluma avocado cultivar.jpg

size.note: The species has a very broad cultivar range; 12 cm is an illustrative example, not a species mean.

cards.name: Olive
cards.origin: Mediterranean and Near Eastern cultivation heritage

location.label: Mediterranean and Near Eastern cultivation heritage

cards.availabilityBand: Fresh: specialty markets; cured olives are widely traded
cards.flavor: Savory and tangy when cured; raw fruit is bitter
cards.texture: Firm to tender flesh around a hard stone
cards.fact: Olives are usually cured before eating to reduce their natural bitterness. Like cherries, they have a stone inside.

weight.note: The Manzanilla de Sevilla cultivar averaged 4.0 g per whole, uncured fruit in a study covering 2012–2020 harvests. Weight is before curing, unlike the flavor description.

cards.imageAlt: Close-up of green olives growing on a leafy branch

size.note: Whole ripe-fruit length, including the stone; cultivars can differ.

cards.name: Plantain
cards.origin: Southeast Asian and New Guinean ancestry; staple in many tropical regions

location.label: Southeast Asian and New Guinean ancestry; staple in many tropical regions

cards.flavor: Starchy when green, sweeter when ripe and cooked
cards.texture: Firm raw flesh that softens with cooking
cards.fact: Plantains are cooking bananas. As they ripen, some of their starch changes into sugar.

weight.note: Kerala Agricultural University lists 250 g per fruit for the Big Ebanga plantain clone. A whole-fruit cultivar example; flavor ratings describe ripe cooked plantain.

size.note: A Brazilian field study reports an average fruit length of 25 cm for its French plantain group; this is a study-specific example, including peel.

cards.name: Asian Pear
cards.texture: Crunchy and very juicy, even when ripe
cards.fact: An Asian pear can look round like an apple, but it is a pear, not an apple-pear hybrid.

weight.note: The Hosui Asian pear control group averaged 241 g per fruit in an irrigation study. A cultivar and treatment sample, not a universal average.

size.note: NC State describes 3–4 inch fruit; this is a rounded Asian-pear example with the stalk excluded.

cards.name: Sour Cherry
cards.texture: Tender, juicy flesh around a hard stone
cards.fact: Sour cherries are especially popular in pies and preserves because their tart flavor balances added sweetness.

weight.note: Rounded from the National Fruit Collection measurement of 4.70 g for the Montmorency sour-cherry cultivar. Includes the stone.

cards.imageAlt: Red Morello sour cherries on stems with water droplets on their skins

size.note: NC State describes round fruits with length and width below one inch (2.54 cm); 2 cm is an illustrative example, excluding the stalk.

cards.name: Greengage
cards.origin: Middle Eastern ancestry; European cultivation heritage

location.label: Middle Eastern ancestry; European cultivation heritage

cards.texture: Juicy, tender flesh around a stone
cards.fact: Many greengages stay green even when ripe and sweet, so a green skin does not always mean an unripe plum.

weight.note: Rounded from the National Fruit Collection measurement of 30.90 g for Belgian Greengage. A whole-fruit cultivar example.

cards.imageAlt: Three green-gold greengage plums against a white background

size.note: Diameter of one round-oval greengage, excluding its stalk.

cards.name: Persian Lime
cards.origin: Hybrid origin uncertain; Tahiti cultivation heritage

location.label: Hybrid origin uncertain; Tahiti cultivation heritage

cards.texture: Juicy flesh under a thin green rind
cards.fact: Persian limes, also called Tahiti limes, are usually larger and less seedy than Key limes.

weight.note: UF/IFAS gives 1.9 oz (54 g) as the typical whole-fruit weight for Tahiti/Persian lime. Fruit size varies by crop and harvest.

cards.sourceFile: Starr-140117-3997-Citrus latifolia-Tahitian fruit and leaves-Hawea Pl Olinda-Maui (24612312943).jpg

size.note: The source gives height 5–7.5 cm and width 4–6.25 cm; the example follows the longer axis.

cards.name: Golden Kiwifruit
cards.origin: Chinese ancestry; modern New Zealand breeding heritage

location.label: Chinese ancestry; modern New Zealand breeding heritage

cards.flavor: Sweet with a gentle tropical tang
cards.texture: Soft yellow flesh with tiny black seeds
cards.fact: Golden kiwifruit varieties have yellow flesh, unlike the familiar green-fleshed kiwifruit.

weight.note: Rounded from 98.3 g, the mean of 1,940 Hort16A golden kiwifruit harvested in May 1995 in New Zealand and reported in the plant patent. A cultivar sample.

size.note: The Hort16A patent gives fruit length 79.1 mm; rounded to 7.9 cm. This named cultivar example is not an average for all yellow-fleshed kiwifruit.
